deep.reconstruction:
The folio holds four separate notes. The middle two are pasted-in slips.

(1) Lie vs. Helmholtz (space problem). Hilbert notes that Lie showed one may not carry the properties of the finite (continuous) group over to the 'verkürzte lineare' group. That group is the linear group induced at a fixed point on the first-order differentials, i.e. the linearized isotropy group. Helmholtz, reasoning as a physicist, had tacitly made this transfer. The reference is Lie–Engel, Theorie der Transformationsgruppen III (1893), Abt. V on the Helmholtz–Lie space problem, pp. 454, 456–460, 505–506. There is no computation, only a bibliographic and critical remark. It forms the background to Hilbert's own 1902 treatment of the space problem without differentiability assumptions.

(2) Kirchhoff's proof of unique continuation of the potential. The claim at issue is that a harmonic function vanishing on an open subregion vanishes throughout the connected domain. My reconstruction of the criticized method (inferred, not stated on the page): take a point on the boundary of the zero region. Choose a circle whose centre lies in the zero region and whose periphery enters the non-zero region only where u has one sign. The mean value property, u(centre) = 0 = mean of u over the periphery, with a one-signed integrand that is not identically zero, then gives a contradiction.

Hilbert objects that such a circle need not exist. His model is f(x,y) = e^{-1/x^2} sin(1/x) for x>0 and f = 0 for x ≤ 0. The exponent is possibly x^4; either works. This f is C^∞ and vanishes identically on the half-plane x ≤ 0. For x>0 it changes sign on the strips 1/((k+1)π) < x < 1/(kπ), which accumulate at the line x=0.

The argument (my filling): any circle whose periphery meets both x ≤ 0 and x > 0 is connected, so it passes through points with arbitrarily small x>0. It therefore meets strips of both signs. Hence its periphery never lies in 'only positive or only negative' territory.

The example is not harmonic. It shows only that the geometric step is not a general fact about sign distributions and needs a justification using harmonicity. Hilbert adds that the same gap occurs in Korn (presumably his Lehrbuch der Potentialtheorie) and in Gauss, 'Allgemeine Lehrsätze…' (Werke Bd. 5, p. 200).

(3) Non-Jordan separating curve. A Jordan curve is a continuous, double-point-free curve x=x(t), y=y(t). Hilbert remarks that a closed set that is not such a curve can still separate the plane into exactly two domains. His figure shows a loop closed up through an oscillating piece x = sin(1/t), y = t (t → 0), which accumulates on a limit segment. In modern terms this is the Warsaw circle: a topologist's sine curve closed by an arc. It is compact and connected but not locally connected, so it is not a continuous image of a circle. Yet its complement has exactly two components. So the converse of the Jordan curve theorem fails without extra hypotheses such as local connectedness or accessibility (Schoenflies).

(4) Identity of geometries. Two geometries count as identical if there is a bijection between their elements under which all theorems of one hold in the other, i.e. an isomorphism of models. For example, the points of Euclidean geometry can be mapped bijectively onto a line segment, provided all axioms are transported along (continued on the next page). Hence a geometry does not depend on how its elements are named. This is Hilbert's well-known axiomatic and structural standpoint.
errors: No mathematical error by Hilbert. One clarification: the counterexample function is not harmonic. It refutes only the unproved geometric step in Kirchhoff's argument (existence of a one-signed circle), not the unique continuation theorem itself, which is true because harmonic functions are real-analytic. Hilbert's wording ('Beweismethode … unrichtig') is consistent with this.

The phrase 'man nicht einen Kreis so legen kann' must be read as concerning circles that meet both the zero region and its complement. Small circles lying entirely inside one strip x∈(1/((k+1)π),1/(kπ)) are one-signed.

results.what: Remark that the properties of the finite continuous group cannot be transferred to its linearized ('verkürzte lineare') isotropy group; this is Lie's critique of Helmholtz's space-problem argument
results.modern_name: Helmholtz–Lie space problem (Lie's correction of Helmholtz)

results.what: Criticism of the Kirchhoff (also Gauss, Korn) mean-value/circle argument for unique continuation of potentials, via the flat C^∞ example e^{-1/x^2} sin(1/x)
results.modern_name: Unique continuation for harmonic functions; flat smooth function with infinitely oscillating sign near the boundary of its zero set
results.usually_credited_to: Flat function: Cauchy (1823). Gaps in Gauss's 1840 potential-theory arguments were noted by various 19th/early-20th-century critics; I cannot confirm specific names.

results.what: A compact connected set that is not a Jordan curve (closed topologist's sine curve) still separates the plane into two domains
results.modern_name: Warsaw circle; failure of the converse of the Jordan curve theorem without local connectedness
results.usually_credited_to: Schoenflies (c. 1900–1908) for such examples and the converse theorem. The name 'Warsaw circle' comes from the Polish school (1920s–30s).

results.what: Two geometries are identical if their elements correspond bijectively so that all theorems carry over; e.g. Euclidean points mapped onto a segment, with the axioms transported
results.modern_name: Isomorphism of models / structural view of axiomatics
results.usually_credited_to: D. Hilbert (Grundlagen der Geometrie 1899; letters to Frege)

deep.surprise_reason: These are lecture-style critical remarks and standard examples of c. 1900. Hilbert's criticism of Gauss/Kirchhoff on unique continuation and the Warsaw-circle-type example are nice unpublished details. However, closely related examples were in Schoenflies' work of the same period, and the axiomatic remark is well known as Hilbert's.

checkable.asserts: The example tends to 0 from the right, matching the zero extension (continuity). Expected value: 0.

checkable.sympy: [limit(diff(exp(-1/x**2)*sin(1/x), x, n), x, 0, '+') for n in range(1,4)]
checkable.asserts: The first derivatives also tend to 0 at 0+, so the glued function is smooth (flat) at x=0. Expected: [0, 0, 0].
sin(1/x) vanishes at x = 1/(k*pi) for integer k (with k declared integer), so the sign changes accumulate at x=0.
At x = 2/((2k+1)π) the sign alternates +1, -1, +1, ... arbitrarily close to x=0.

transcription_corrections: The exponent in e^{-1/x^…} is hard to read. It may be x^4 (or x^{(4)}) rather than x^2. Mathematically either works.
In the struck passage, 'Beispiel' is crossed out and 'Gebiet fällt' follows. The inserted '(der Potentialfunktion)' is written above the line at the top right of the slip.
The figure label reads 'sin 1/t = x', attached by an arrow to the oscillating part of the closed curve.
'verkürzte' appears correct ('die verkürzte lineare' = linearized/reduced group), not a misreading.
